prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit ubiquitin ligases such as cereblon to mark chosen proteins for destruction, from the first PROTACs to the mechanism of thalidomide-class molecular glues

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single prize part for targeted protein degradation, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa. The unifying principle is chemically induced proximity to a ubiquitin ligase: a small molecule converts the cell's own degradation machinery into a reagent, and pharmacology becomes catalytic and event-driven instead of occupancy-driven. This reaches proteins with no active site, which is what researchers and clinicians could not do before. Crews and Deshaies established the bifunctional concept and showed it works in cells. Handa's identification of cereblon as the thalidomide target showed that the same hijacking is how a drug class already in use works, and it supplied the ligase handle that most degraders now use. The mechanism has been reproduced across many ligases and targets by independent groups, and degraders are in clinical trials. It is the only position four members support, and I hold it for the science, not for the count.
statement.case_against: No PROTAC drug is approved, as far as I know, so clinical vindication is incomplete and a majority could reasonably call this early. The cereblon result is target identification and mechanism, and Somfai is right that it is closer to chemical biology than to a new reaction or synthetic method. A single citation joining PROTACs and glues can sound like two stapled discoveries. A three-person cap excludes Ciulli (VHL ligands, ternary-complex structures), Sakamoto (first PROTAC paper), Gray, Ito and Kim, and any choice here is contestable.

responses.point: Somfai places Buchwald-Hartwig C-N coupling first for its clean attribution and mechanistic detail, and asks what was new chemically in the cereblon discovery compared with chemical biology.
responses.response: I accept that Buchwald-Hartwig has the cleanest attribution and the longest confirmation on the shortlist, and the 2010 overlap is real but not disqualifying. My answer on what is chemically new is that the degradation prize rests on more than target identification. Crews and Deshaies built a heterobifunctional molecule whose design rules (linker, ternary-complex cooperativity, ligase choice) are explicit chemistry. Handa's cereblon work explains how a small molecule remodels a ligase surface so that new substrates, the neosubstrates, are ubiquitinated. That is a molecular mechanism, not just a name for a target. I still see degradation as the larger change in what chemists can make, and I think the 2010 overlap weighs more against B011 than the identification issue weighs against B044.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, supports the same three names and a single unifying citation, and warns that joining PROTACs with the cereblon molecular-glue mechanism risks sounding like two discoveries stapled together.
responses.response: I agree and I have tightened my citation to answer your question. The principle is recruiting a ubiquitin ligase to a chosen protein, and the wording says that PROTACs and glues are two routes to it, so the lay reader can see why Handa stands beside Crews and Deshaies without implying that cereblon work is PROTAC chemistry. On what Handa adds beyond target identification, he gave the field the first validated ligase handle and the explanation of why thalidomide analogues degrade specific proteins, which is why cereblon ligands are used in so many degraders. I do not claim more than that. If the committee cannot accept Handa's inclusion, I would rather drop to two names than put in a weaker third.

responses.point: Chabes proposes two parts, base editing for Liu alone and degradation for Crews and Deshaies, and would accept Handa as a third name only if the committee prefers one achievement.
responses.response: I take your pairing seriously as a coherent chemical-biology theme, and I thank you for naming Handa as acceptable. I still prefer one part. The Liu-alone attribution is contested by Aqvist, Brzezinski, Linke, Somfai and me because Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida all have claims, and the 2020 overlap worries several of us. A two-part prize with a disputed second half would weaken a degradation part that can stand alone. Leaving Handa out also drops the only explanation of how thalidomide works, which is why I would keep three names and one part.

responses.point: Sparr prefers biomolecular phase separation as a physical-chemical organizing principle, while acknowledging it may not reach five votes and that condensate physiology is still debated.
responses.response: I find the thermodynamic framing compelling and I know your work on self-assembly gives you more authority than I have on this. My concern is the one you partly share: the in-cell equilibrium-phase question is open, and the committee would be crediting a framework whose scope is still being measured. Degradation has a narrower claim but one that is settled in mechanism. I would revisit B039 in a later year once those measurements are in.

uncertainties: Whether a majority treats the absence of an approved PROTAC drug as disqualifying this year (not independently verified).
Whether Handa or Ciulli should hold the third place, and how Ito, Sakamoto, Gray and Kim are weighed against the three-person cap.
Whether one citation can unify PROTACs and cereblon glues without blurring two origins.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. I know Emma Sparr's research on self-assembly, but it does not involve a shortlisted candidate or credited name. None of my postdoc mentors or Linkoping colleagues is among the credited names. Nothing in round 1 changes this.
